opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a very liberating way to look at research. In a lot of careers you're evaluated by your average: how consistent you are, whether you hit your targets every quarter. Research doesn't really work like that. Nobody remembers the ten papers that were just okay. People remember the one idea that changed how the field thinks, the one that other people built on for years.

That changes how you should behave. If you're judged by your peak, failure becomes cheap. You can try risky things, spend a year on something that might not work, and it doesn't drag down your "score." The only real risk is never trying anything big. So it pushes you toward ambition rather than safety. You don't have to optimize for a steady stream of incremental results. You can afford to be a little stubborn, a little contrarian, and chase the questions you actually find important.

It's also more honest about how progress happens. Breakthroughs are heavy-tailed. A small number of ideas account for most of the impact. If the evaluation system matched that reality, rewarding the highest point, students and young researchers would stop feeling they need to publish constantly just to prove they're productive. I'd rather someone spend three years and produce one thing that really matters than fifteen papers nobody reads.

Of course, there's a caveat. To reach a high point you still need a lot of accumulation underneath: the experiments that failed, the intuition you built, the taste you developed. So it's not that the rest doesn't matter. It's that the rest is in service of the peak. Seen that way, all the messy, unglamorous work stops being a burden and becomes part of the search. I find that very freeing, and I think it's a healthier mindset for doing research.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a researcher can spend years pursuing one impactful idea and that evaluation rewards the peak rather than a steady stream of results, communicating that one major success can be enough.

r002.rationale: The response discusses ambition, risk-taking, and research progress, but does not frame research as an infinite game.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the kindest properties of this profession, honestly. In most jobs you're evaluated on your average. If you have a bad quarter, a bad year, it drags everything down. Research doesn't work that way. Nobody remembers that you had three papers rejected in 2019. They remember the one idea that actually changed how people think about something.

What that means practically is that you're allowed to fail. Not just allowed, you're kind of expected to. If I look back at my own work, the vast majority of things I tried didn't go anywhere, or they were incremental, or they were fine but forgettable. That's normal. The ones that mattered, like ResNeXt or the ConvNeXt work or some of the more recent stuff on representation learning, those came out of a long stretch of things that looked like nothing was happening. If I had been judged on the average, I would have looked mediocre most of the time.

And I think it changes your psychology as a researcher. If your average matters, you become conservative. You pick safe problems, you optimize for the paper count, you avoid anything that might take two years and produce zero. But if only the peak matters, then the rational strategy is to take big swings. You can afford to spend a year on something weird because the downside is bounded and the upside is unbounded.

So when students come to me and they're anxious about a rejection, or they feel like they're behind because someone in their cohort has more papers, I try to tell them this. The game isn't to never fail. The game is to put yourself in a position where, when you do hit, it's something real. One great thing beats ten good things. And the only way to get one great thing is to be willing to produce a lot of things that aren't.

r001.rationale: The response says research is judged by its peak, that one great contribution can outweigh many lesser ones, and that a researcher needs to keep trying until they produce something that matters.

r002.rationale: It uses “game” as a metaphor for taking risks and recovering from failure, but does not frame research as an infinite game.

astra-6.text:
Because it gives you room to fail. You can try ten ideas, and maybe nine of them go nowhere, but if the tenth really changes how people think about a problem, that contribution matters. The unsuccessful attempts don’t cancel it out.

I think that’s a healthy incentive for research, because research is inherently uncertain. If you were judged by your average result, you’d be tempted to choose safe problems where you could reliably produce something. When your strongest contribution matters most, you have more freedom to take a risk and spend time on something that might not work.

And it’s encouraging on a personal level, too. A period when nothing works doesn’t have to define your career. You can keep exploring, and your best work can still be ahead of you.

r001.rationale: The response says many attempts can fail while one contribution that changes how people think can still matter most, communicating that a researcher needs to succeed once.

r002.rationale: The response describes research as uncertain and encourages continued exploration, but does not frame it as an infinite game.

sol-6.1.text:
Because it gives you room to fail. Research is inherently uncertain, and if you’re judged by the average of everything you do, you’re encouraged to play it safe—to keep producing things that you know will work. But the work that really moves a field forward often comes from taking a risk, and most of those attempts won’t succeed.

If one important contribution can define your career, you can spend time exploring something difficult without worrying that every unsuccessful experiment lowers your score. That’s a very positive incentive. It encourages you to ask, “What’s the most meaningful thing I could work on?” rather than, “What can I reliably publish next?”

r001.rationale: It says one important contribution can define a career, while unsuccessful attempts need not lower the researcher’s standing—communicating that one success can be enough.

r002.rationale: The response describes research as uncertain and encourages risk-taking, but does not frame research as an infinite game.
